plan: Natural science passage of about 520 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000024) on Tambora and the Year Without a Summer; one thesis item only (main purpose); two hard items (timing synthesis; qualified attitude).

passages.title: The Year Without a Summer
passages.text:
In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with a force that dwarfed anything in recorded history. The explosion killed thousands of people on the island and in the surrounding seas, and it hurled ash and gas high into the atmosphere. Then, for a time, nothing unusual seemed to happen elsewhere in the world. The strangest consequences arrived more than a year later and half a planet away.

The eruption had injected enormous amounts of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, well above the level where rain could wash it out. There the gas formed a thin haze of tiny droplets that spread around the globe and reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space. The cooling it caused was modest when averaged over the whole Northern Hemisphere, less than one degree Celsius. But averages can hide a great deal.

In New England, snow fell in June 1816, and hard frosts returned in July and August, killing corn and other crops just as they began to ripen. In parts of Europe, cold, relentless rain rotted the harvest in the fields. Grain prices soared, and in some regions food riots broke out. Farmers who had never thought about the upper atmosphere found their year ruined by it. Few people in Europe or North America had even heard of the eruption, and no one yet understood how a volcano could change the weather an ocean away; many blamed sunspots, or simply bad luck.

The year 1816 came to be called the Year Without a Summer, and it shows something that a single average figure cannot. A small drop in mean temperature matters less than when the cold arrives. A few unseasonable frosts in the middle of the growing season can destroy a crop that would have survived a winter several degrees colder than usual.

The cold summer also left a cultural trace. Kept indoors by storms at a villa near Lake Geneva, a group of young English writers held a contest to see who could write the most frightening story, and Mary Shelley began the novel that became Frankenstein. It is tempting to say that the volcano produced the novel, and the story is often told that way. It would be more accurate to say that the weather supplied the occasion; the ideas were already Shelley's own.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: explain why volcanoes in Indonesia erupt more violently than volcanoes elsewhere.
choices.B: describe the eruption's distant effects and what they reveal about climate.
choices.C: argue that Frankenstein would not have been written without the eruption.
choices.D: compare the damage the eruption caused on Sumbawa with the damage in Europe.

candidates.evidence: it shows something that a single average figure cannot
candidates.explanation: The passage traces the eruption's distant effects in 1816 and draws a lesson about averages and timing; a final paragraph adds a cultural footnote.

A.rationale: The passage does not compare volcanoes.

C.rationale: The author rejects the claim that the volcano produced the novel.

D.rationale: The passage mentions local deaths only briefly and makes no such comparison.

hints: What does most of the passage describe, and what lesson does it draw?
candidates.remember: A main-purpose answer covers the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the eruption cooled the Northern Hemisphere mainly because:

choices.A: ash from the eruption blocked rain clouds from forming.
choices.B: the explosion released cold air from deep inside the volcano.
choices.C: sunspots reduced the amount of light reaching Earth.
choices.D: sulfur droplets reflected some sunlight back into space.

candidates.evidence: reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that sulfur gas formed droplets that "reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space."

A.rationale: The passage says the sulfur haze reflected sunlight; it does not mention ash and clouds this way.

B.rationale: Nothing in the passage supports this.

C.rationale: Sunspots are what some people mistakenly blamed.

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence about how the haze affected sunlight.

candidates.remember: Distinguish the stated cause from causes people wrongly blamed.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "modest" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: The cooling was "less than one degree Celsius" on average, so "modest" means small.

B.rationale: "Humble" describes a person's attitude, not a temperature change.

C.rationale: "Decent" in the sense of proper does not describe a temperature change.

D.rationale: The author is describing the size of the cooling, not judging whether it was reasonable.

hints: What size of change does the sentence describe?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with "small" and check.

candidates.remember: Words about people can describe amounts in a different sense.

candidates.stem: The main function of paragraph 3 is to:

choices.A: explain the chemistry of the sulfur haze in more detail.
choices.B: show that the eruption's effects were limited to New England.
choices.C: give concrete examples of the harm that the small average cooling caused.
choices.D: introduce the writers who gathered near Lake Geneva.

candidates.evidence: In New England, snow fell in June 1816
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends by saying "averages can hide a great deal"; paragraph 3 shows what they hid: June snow, summer frosts, rotted harvests and food riots.

A.rationale: Paragraph 3 describes effects on farms and food, not chemistry.

hints: How does paragraph 3 follow from the last sentence of paragraph 2?

strategy.explanation: Connect the end of paragraph 2 to paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: A paragraph of examples often follows a general claim.

candidates.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from paragraph 3 that most people affected by the cold summer of 1816:

choices.A: blamed the eruption for their ruined crops.
choices.B: did not know what had caused the unusual weather.
choices.C: expected the cold to last for many years.
choices.D: had studied the upper atmosphere before 1816.

candidates.evidence: no one yet understood how a volcano could change the weather an ocean away
candidates.explanation: Few people had heard of the eruption, no one understood the mechanism, and many blamed sunspots or luck, so most did not know the true cause.

A.rationale: The passage says few had heard of the eruption and many blamed sunspots or bad luck.

D.rationale: The passage says farmers "had never thought about the upper atmosphere."

hints: What did people blame for the weather?
candidates.remember: An inference must fit every detail the passage gives.

candidates.subskill: Synthesizing a claim about averages and timing
candidates.stem: Based on paragraphs 2 through 4, the author suggests that the cooling of 1816 was so destructive mainly because:

choices.A: cold weather struck during the growing season, when crops were most vulnerable.
choices.B: average temperatures fell by several degrees across the Northern Hemisphere.
choices.C: the winter of 1815–1816 was several degrees colder than usual.
choices.D: farmers had planted crops that could not tolerate any cold at all.

candidates.evidence: A small drop in mean temperature matters less than when the cold arrives.
candidates.explanation: The author stresses that the average drop was small but that frosts "in the middle of the growing season" destroyed crops: timing, not size, made the cooling destructive.

B.rationale: The author says the average drop was less than one degree.

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 says crops could survive a much colder winter; the damage came from summer frosts.

D.rationale: Nothing is said about the kinds of crops chosen.

hints: Does the author emphasize how much it cooled or when?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that contradict the small average or the winter comparison.

candidates.remember: Connect a general claim to the evidence that supports it.

author_checklist.hardness: Two distractors use the passage's own numbers and the winter comparison in ways that sound right but reverse the author's point; the answer requires combining paragraphs 2 and 4.

candidates.stem: The final paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: return to the science of the eruption and summarize it.
choices.B: prove that bad weather is necessary for great literature.
choices.C: explain why food riots broke out in Europe.
choices.D: add a cultural consequence and qualify a popular claim about it.

candidates.evidence: The cold summer also left a cultural trace.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph adds a cultural consequence (the writing contest) and then qualifies the claim that the volcano produced the novel.

A.rationale: The final paragraph discusses a novel, not the science.

B.rationale: The author makes no such general claim.

hints: What new kind of consequence does the last paragraph introduce?

strategy.explanation: Look at the paragraph's first and last sentences.

candidates.remember: Closing paragraphs often widen the scope or qualify a claim.

withdrawn.reason: Both solvers: R024-07's key ('qualify a popular claim') and R024-08's key ('skeptical') give each other away; R024-08 (also rated easy against a hard label) withdrawn before review.

item.subskill: Author's view of a popular claim
item.stem: The author's view of the idea that the volcano "produced" Frankenstein is best described as:

choices.A: accepting, since the storms kept the writers indoors.
choices.B: skeptical: the weather gave Shelley an occasion, not her ideas.
choices.C: dismissive, since the author doubts the writing contest took place.
choices.D: undecided, since the author says the evidence is evenly balanced.

item.evidence: the weather supplied the occasion; the ideas were already Shelley's own
item.explanation: The author grants the weather's role in creating the occasion but rejects the stronger claim that the volcano produced the novel.

A.rationale: The author calls the claim tempting but says it would be "more accurate" to say the weather only supplied the occasion.

C.rationale: The author treats the contest as fact.

D.rationale: The author states a clear view.

hints: What does the author say would be "more accurate"?
item.remember: "It is tempting to say X" usually introduces a claim the author will qualify.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice A states a true detail (the storms kept the writers indoors) as if it supported the claim; students must see the author grants the detail but rejects the conclusion.
